hops.title: Say it: same herd, different stripes
hops.text: "Same herd, different stripes!" Grown-up zebras are usually black and white, and each zebra's stripe pattern is its own, like a fingerprint. A Grevy's zebra has about 80 stripes. Save the phrase for after the ruler comes out, when your child finds peas or puppies that match in big ways and differ in small ones.

sources.citation: Natural History Museum of Los Angeles County, Spotting Species with Zebra Stripes in the Mammalogy Collection (2025)
Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, Grevy's Zebra
Lincoln Park Zoo, Endangered Grevy's Zebra Born at Lincoln Park Zoo

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A black-and-white mother zebra stands beside her brown-and-white foal. They have different stripe patterns.
image.caption: Every zebra wears stripes, yet no two stripe patterns match.

hops.title: Point at it: sun leaves and shade leaves on one tree
hops.text: Stand with your child under one leafy tree you know is safe. Look closely at leaves tucked deep in the shady lower branches, then at leaves out in the bright sun. On the very same tree, shade leaves often grow larger and thinner, while sun leaves stay smaller and thicker.

sources.citation: Stephen G. Saupe, Plant Physiology (Biology 327) leaf lab, College of Saint Benedict and Saint John's University
USA National Phenology Network, Sun Leaves

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A parent and child seen from behind under one leafy tree, comparing larger shade leaves below with smaller sun leaves above.
image.caption: Even on one tree, leaves that grow in shade can be larger and thinner than leaves that grow in sun.

hops.title: Ask it: how do gray flamingo chicks turn pink?
hops.text: Tell your child that flamingo chicks hatch with white-gray fluff and straight bills, then ask, "How do you think they turn pink like their parents?" Kids may guess sunshine, paint or just growing up. Welcome every guess, then share the surprise: over several years, pigments from the algae and brine shrimp they eat turn them pink.

sources.citation: Smithsonian's National Zoo and Conservation Biology Institute, Why Are Flamingos Pink? And Other Flamingo Facts

image.alt: AI-generated illustration: A bright pink adult flamingo with a curved bill standing beside a fluffy white-gray chick with a straight bill.
image.caption: Flamingo chicks hatch gray and turn pink over several years from what they eat.

audio.title: Three playful ways to talk about living things that are alike, not identical
audio.transcript: Hey there! Before you open the pea pods and line up the leaves, here are three playful ways to keep the big idea going all week. First, a catchphrase: "Same herd, different stripes!" Grown-up zebras are usually black and white, and each zebra's stripe pattern is its own, kind of like a fingerprint. A Grevy's zebra has about eighty stripes in all. Save the phrase for after your child has measured the peas, then pull it out whenever two puppies in a storybook, or two peas from one pod, match in big ways and differ in small ones. Next, a tree to stand under. On your next walk, stop with your child beside one leafy tree you know is safe. Look closely at the leaves tucked deep in the shady lower branches, then at the leaves out in the bright sun. On the very same tree, shade leaves often grow larger and thinner, while sun leaves stay smaller and thicker. Same tree, different leaves, partly from how much light they got. Finally, a wonder question for the car. Tell your child that flamingo chicks hatch with fluffy white-gray feathers and straight bills, then ask, "How do you think they turn pink like their parents?" Kids come up with wonderful guesses, from sunshine to paint to magic. Enjoy every answer before you share the twist: flamingos turn pink over several years, from natural pigments in the algae and brine shrimp they eat. Have fun spotting surprises together!
